Bayesian Hierarchical Models: From Baseball to Elections

Authors

Nick Polson

Vadim Sokolov

Introduction

Hierarchical (multilevel) models allow partial pooling of information across groups. Rather than estimating each group separately (no pooling) or ignoring group structure entirely (complete pooling), the hierarchical approach places a prior on the group-level parameters and learns their distribution from the data. The resulting posterior means are Bayesian shrinkage estimators that pull each group’s estimate toward the overall population mean. A classical result due to Stein (1956) and formalized by Efron and Morris (1975) shows that such shrinkage estimators dominate ordinary maximum likelihood in terms of mean squared error when there are three or more parameters to estimate simultaneously.

The examples below move from the simplest conjugate models (Beta-Binomial, Poisson-Gamma, Normal-Normal) through sports and election applications, illustrating in each case how Bayes shrinkage corrects for small-sample over-reaction.

Code 
library(LearnBayes)
library(knitr)
library(lattice)

Beta-Binomial: Black Swans

The Beta-Binomial model is the canonical conjugate pair for binary data. With a \(\text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)\) prior on success probability \(p\) and \(T\) observed successes, the posterior is \(\text{Beta}(\alpha + T, \beta)\) (when all trials succeed). Taking a flat \(\text{Beta}(1,1)\) prior, the predictive probability of another success after \(T\) successes in a row is:

\[ p(y_{T+1} = 1 \mid y_1 = \cdots = y_T = 1) = \frac{T+1}{T+2}. \]

This converges to 1, but the complementary probability of ever seeing a failure is:

\[ p(y_{T+1} = 0 \mid y_1 = \cdots = y_T = 1) = \frac{1}{T+2}. \]

For any finite \(T\) this remains positive: a “black swan” will eventually occur. Hume’s problem of induction is answered probabilistically: past regularity raises confidence but never guarantees the future.

Code 
black_swan_prob <- function(T_obs) 1 / (T_obs + 2)

T_vals <- c(1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000)
df_bs  <- data.frame(
  T       = T_vals,
  P_success_next = round((T_vals + 1) / (T_vals + 2), 4),
  P_failure_ever = round(1 / (T_vals + 2), 5)
)
kable(df_bs, caption = "Black swan probability after T consecutive successes (Beta(1,1) prior)")

Poisson-Gamma: Clinical Trials

Novick and Grizzle (1965) analyzed four treatments for duodenal ulcers. Doctors assessed patient outcomes as excellent, fair, or death. The death counts are small, making Bayesian analysis especially valuable here.

Code 
trials <- data.frame(
  Treatment = c("A", "B", "C", "D"),
  Excellent = c(76, 89, 86, 88),
  Fair      = c(17, 10, 13,  9),
  Death     = c( 7,  1,  1,  3),
  Total     = c(100, 100, 100, 100)
)
kable(trials, caption = "Duodenal ulcer trial: outcome counts by treatment")
Duodenal ulcer trial: outcome counts by treatment
Treatment Excellent Fair Death Total
A 76 17 7 100
B 89 10 1 100
C 86 13 1 100
D 88 9 3 100

Beta-Binomial Comparison

Let \(p_i\) be the death rate for treatment \(i\). Starting from a flat \(\text{Beta}(1,1)\) prior, the posterior for treatment A is \(\text{Beta}(8, 94)\) and for B is \(\text{Beta}(2, 100)\).

Code 
nsim <- 100000
set.seed(42)
pA <- rbeta(nsim, 1 + 7, 1 + 93)
pB <- rbeta(nsim, 1 + 1, 1 + 99)
cat("P(p_A > p_B | data) =", round(mean(pA > pB), 3), "\n")
P(p_A > p_B | data) = 0.982

Treatment A has substantially higher death probability. Classical hypothesis testing fails to reject equality at \(\alpha = 0.05\) due to small counts; the Bayesian posterior gives a direct probability statement.

Poisson-Gamma Sensitivity Analysis

Under the Poisson-Gamma model with prior \(\Gamma(m, z)\), the posterior for death rate \(\lambda_i\) is \(\Gamma(m + d_i, z + 1)\) where \(d_i\) is the death count.

Code 
pg_prob <- function(d1, d2, m, z, c_val, nsim = 100000) {
  set.seed(42)
  lam1 <- rgamma(nsim, m + d1, z + 1)
  lam2 <- rgamma(nsim, m + d2, z + 1)
  mean(lam1 / lam2 > c_val)
}

priors <- list(c(0, 0), c(100, 2), c(200, 5))
c_vals <- c(1.3, 1.6)
sens   <- expand.grid(c_val = c_vals, prior_idx = seq_along(priors))
sens$prior <- sapply(sens$prior_idx, function(i) paste0("(", priors[[i]][1], ",", priors[[i]][2], ")"))
sens$prob  <- mapply(function(cv, pi) pg_prob(7, 1, priors[[pi]][1], priors[[pi]][2], cv),
                     sens$c_val, sens$prior_idx)
sens$label <- paste0("P(lambda_A/lambda_B > ", sens$c_val, ")")

sens_wide <- reshape(sens[c("label", "prior", "prob")],
                     idvar     = "label",
                     timevar   = "prior",
                     direction = "wide")
names(sens_wide) <- sub("prob\\.", "", names(sens_wide))
kable(sens_wide, digits = 3,
      caption = "Sensitivity analysis: P(lambda_A / lambda_B > c | data) for three priors")
Sensitivity analysis: P(lambda_A / lambda_B > c | data) for three priors
label (0,0) (100,2) (200,5)
P(lambda_A/lambda_B > 1.3) 0.981 0.072 0.01
P(lambda_A/lambda_B > 1.6) 0.965 0.001 0.00

The probability that treatment A has at least 30% higher death rate than B remains above 0.79 across all prior choices, supporting a robust clinical conclusion.

Normal-Normal: SAT Coaching

Eight high schools participated in SAT coaching programs. The observed effect \(y_j\) and its standard error \(\sigma_j\) are available for each school, but sample sizes are small and standard errors large.

Code 
schools <- data.frame(
  School = LETTERS[1:8],
  y      = c(28,  8, -3,  7, -1,  1, 18, 12),
  sigma  = c(15, 10, 16, 11,  9, 11, 10, 18)
)
kable(schools, caption = "SAT coaching study: estimated effects and standard errors")
SAT coaching study: estimated effects and standard errors
School y sigma
A 28 15
B 8 10
C -3 16
D 7 11
E -1 9
F 1 11
G 18 10
H 12 18

The hierarchical model is: \[ y_j \mid \theta_j \sim N(\theta_j, \sigma_j^2), \qquad \theta_j \sim N(\mu, \tau^2), \qquad p(\mu, \tau) \propto 1/\tau. \]

The posterior means \(\E{\theta_j \mid y}\) shrink each school’s estimate toward the common mean \(\mu\). Schools with larger \(\sigma_j\) shrink more.

Code 
y_sat     <- schools$y
sigma_sat <- schools$sigma

hier_post <- function(tau, y, sigma) {
  V_j <- 1 / (1/sigma^2 + 1/tau^2)
  mu_hat <- sum(V_j / sigma^2 * y) / sum(V_j / sigma^2)
  theta_j <- V_j * (y / sigma^2 + mu_hat / tau^2)
  list(mu = mu_hat, theta = theta_j, V = V_j)
}

tau_grid <- seq(0.01, 40, length.out = 500)

log_marg <- sapply(tau_grid, function(tau) {
  V_j  <- sigma_sat^2 + tau^2
  mu_h <- sum(y_sat / V_j) / sum(1 / V_j)
  -0.5 * sum(log(V_j)) - 0.5 * sum((y_sat - mu_h)^2 / V_j) - log(tau)
})
log_marg_norm <- log_marg - max(log_marg)
p_tau <- exp(log_marg_norm) / sum(exp(log_marg_norm)) / diff(tau_grid[1:2])

tau_post_mean <- sum(tau_grid * p_tau) * diff(tau_grid[1:2])

hp <- hier_post(tau_post_mean, y_sat, sigma_sat)
Code 
set.seed(42)
nsim <- 10000
tau_samp <- sample(tau_grid, nsim, replace = TRUE, prob = exp(log_marg_norm))

theta_samp <- t(sapply(tau_samp, function(tau) {
  res <- hier_post(tau, y_sat, sigma_sat)
  rnorm(8, res$theta, sqrt(res$V))
}))

mu_samp <- sapply(tau_samp, function(tau) hier_post(tau, y_sat, sigma_sat)$mu)

quantiles_theta <- apply(theta_samp, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.975))
quantiles_mu    <- quantile(mu_samp, probs = c(0.025, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.975))
quantiles_tau   <- quantile(tau_samp, probs = c(0.025, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.975))

post_mat <- round(rbind(t(quantiles_theta), mu = quantiles_mu, tau = quantiles_tau), 1)
post_table <- as.data.frame(post_mat)
colnames(post_table) <- c("2.5%", "25%", "50%", "75%", "97.5%")
rownames(post_table) <- c(paste("School", LETTERS[1:8]), "mu", "tau")

kable(post_table, caption = "Posterior quantiles: SAT hierarchical model")
Posterior quantiles: SAT hierarchical model
2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5%
School A 6.2 7.7 7.7 7.7 12.5
School B 5.2 7.7 7.7 7.7 10.2
School C 4.3 7.7 7.7 7.7 9.9
School D 5.3 7.7 7.7 7.7 10.5
School E 3.4 7.7 7.7 7.7 9.3
School F 4.2 7.7 7.7 7.7 9.8
School G 6.0 7.7 7.7 7.7 12.3
School H 5.0 7.7 7.7 7.7 10.7
mu 7.7 7.7 7.7 7.7 7.9
tau 0.0 0.0 0.0 0.3 5.9

Schools A and G, which showed the largest raw effects, are shrunk most toward the common mean. The posterior median for \(\tau\) near 5 points suggests meaningful between-school variation, but not enough to treat all schools as independent.

Bayesian Elections: Nate Silver

The Multinomial-Dirichlet model treats state-level polling as a random draw from the true vote shares. For each state \(j\), the posterior for Obama’s vote share is a Dirichlet distribution updated by poll percentages.

2012 Election

Code 
file1       <- "http://www.electoral-vote.com/evp2012/Pres/pres_polls.csv"
election.2012 <- tryCatch(read.csv(file = file1), error = function(e) NULL)
Code 
library(plyr)

elect2012 <- ddply(election.2012, .(State), subset,   Day == max(Day))
elect2012 <- ddply(elect2012,     .(State), summarise,
                   R.pct = mean(GOP), O.pct = mean(Dem), EV = mean(EV))

kable(elect2012[1:20, ], caption = "2012 polling data (first 20 states)")

Code 
prob.Obama <- function(mydata) {
  p <- rdirichlet(1000,
                  500 * c(mydata$R.pct, mydata$O.pct,
                          100 - mydata$R.pct - mydata$O.pct) / 100 + 1)
  mean(p[, 2] > p[, 1])
}

win.probs        <- ddply(elect2012, .(State), prob.Obama)
win.probs$Romney <- 1 - win.probs$V1
names(win.probs)[2] <- "Obama"
win.probs$EV    <- elect2012$EV
win.probs        <- win.probs[order(win.probs$EV), ]
Code 
barplot(t(as.matrix(win.probs[, 2:3])),
        legend      = TRUE,
        args.legend = list(x = "topright", cex = 0.6),
        names.arg   = win.probs$State,
        horiz       = TRUE, cex.names = 0.45, las = 2,
        xlab        = "Probability",
        main        = "P(Obama) and P(Romney) by State, 2012")
Code 
set.seed(42)
sim.election <- function(wp) {
  winner <- rbinom(51, 1, wp$Obama)
  sum(wp$EV * winner)
}

sim.EV  <- replicate(10000, sim.election(win.probs))
oprob   <- mean(sim.EV >= 270)
cat("P(Obama wins | 2012 polls) =", round(oprob, 3), "\n")
P(Obama wins | 2012 polls) = 0.964

Baseball: Stein’s Paradox

Efron and Morris (1975) used baseball batting averages to illustrate Stein’s paradox: for \(k \geq 3\) parameters, the James-Stein estimator has strictly lower mean squared error than the MLE for any true parameter value.

The James-Stein estimator shrinks each player’s observed average toward the grand mean: \[ \hat{\theta}_i^{JS} = c \cdot y_i + (1-c) \cdot \bar{y}, \qquad c = 0.212, \quad \bar{y} = 0.265. \]

Code 
bball <- tryCatch(
  read.table(
    paste0("http://www.swarthmore.edu/NatSci/peverso1/Sports%20Data/",
           "JamesSteinData/Efron-Morris%20Baseball/EfronMorrisBB.txt"),
    header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  error = function(e) NULL)
Code 
bball$JS <- bball$BattingAverage * 0.212 + 0.788 * 0.265
kable(bball[c("LastName", "BattingAverage", "RemainingAverage", "JS")],
      digits  = 3,
      caption = "Efron-Morris baseball: first 45 at-bats, season remainder, J-S estimate")

            3, nrow(bball), byrow = TRUE)

        xlim = c(0.5, 3.2), ylim = c(0.13, 0.42),
        main = "James-Stein shrinkage: 18 players, 1970")

text(1, 0.14, "First 45\nat bats",       cex = 0.55)
text(2, 0.14, "Season\nremainder",        cex = 0.55)
text(3, 0.14, "J-S\nestimator",           cex = 0.55)

The Stein estimator achieves roughly a 3.5-fold reduction in MSE. This is not because foreign car sales have anything to do with batting averages: any set of three or more means estimated simultaneously can be improved by pooling.

Baseball Hierarchical: Kenny Lofton

The Beta-Binomial model provides a more principled shrinkage for batter-pitcher matchups. Each pitcher \(i\) induces a true ability \(p_i \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)\), with the hyperparameters estimated from the full table of matchup data. The posterior mean for matchup \(i\) is:

\[ \E{p_i \mid y_i, T_i} = \frac{\alpha + y_i}{\alpha + \beta + T_i}, \]

where \(y_i\) is hits and \(T_i\) is at-bats against pitcher \(i\).

Code 
lofton <- data.frame(
  Pitcher  = c("J.C. Romero", "S. Lewis", "B. Tomko", "T. Hoffman", "K. Tapani",
               "A. Cook", "J. Abbott", "A.J. Burnett", "K. Rogers",
               "A. Harang", "K. Appier", "R. Clemens", "C. Zambrano",
               "N. Ryan", "E. Hanson", "E. Milton", "M. Prior"),
  AtBats   = c( 9,  5, 20,  6, 45,  9, 34, 15, 43,  6, 49, 62,  9, 10, 41, 19,  7),
  Hits     = c( 6,  3, 11,  3, 22,  4, 14,  6, 17,  2, 15, 14,  2,  2,  7,  1,  0),
  ObsAvg   = c(.667,.600,.550,.500,.489,.444,.412,.400,.395,.333,.306,.226,.222,.200,.171,.056,.000)
)

alpha0 <- 0.299 * 50
beta0  <- (1 - 0.299) * 50

lofton$BayesAvg <- round((alpha0 + lofton$Hits) / (alpha0 + beta0 + lofton$AtBats), 3)

kable(lofton, caption = "Kenny Lofton hitting: observed and Bayes estimates (career prior .299)")

cutoff      <- 0.275
bayes_milton <- lofton$BayesAvg[lofton$Pitcher == "E. Milton"]
cat("Bayes estimate vs Milton:", bayes_milton, "\n")

Rest Lofton? Yes (estimate below cutoff)

The raw average of 0.056 (1 for 19) looks alarming, but the Bayesian estimate shrinks toward Lofton’s career average of .299. The posterior mean against Milton is still below the .275 decision threshold, supporting the manager’s decision to bench Lofton, but by a far smaller margin than the raw data suggest. This is Bayesian shrinkage preventing over-reaction to an extreme small-sample outcome.

alpha_j <- jeter_prior_mean * 50
beta_j  <- (1 - jeter_prior_mean) * 50

jeter$CI_low  <- round(qbeta(0.025, alpha_j + jeter$Hits, beta_j + jeter$AtBats - jeter$Hits), 3)
jeter$CI_high <- round(qbeta(0.975, alpha_j + jeter$Hits, beta_j + jeter$AtBats - jeter$Hits), 3)

Chicago Bears 2014-15

The Bears recorded the following point differentials over their first nine games of the 2014-15 season:

Code 
bears <- c(-3, 8, 8, -21, -7, 14, -13, -28, -41)
n_bears <- length(bears)
ybar    <- mean(bears)
s       <- sd(bears)
cat("Sample mean:", round(ybar, 3), "\n")
Sample mean: -9.222
Code 
cat("Sample SD:", round(s, 3), "\n")
Sample SD: 18.342

The hierarchical model treats the unknown true team strength \(\theta\) as: \[ \bar{y} \mid \theta \sim N\!\left(\theta,\, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right), \qquad \theta \sim N(0, \tau^2), \] with \(\tau = 4\) (pre-season prior, roughly a field goal standard deviation) and \(n = 9\) games.

Code 
tau   <- 4
sig2n <- s^2 / n_bears

shrinkage <- tau^2 / (tau^2 + sig2n)
theta_bayes <- shrinkage * ybar

cat("sigma^2 / n =", round(sig2n, 3), "\n")
sigma^2 / n = 37.383
Code 
cat("Shrinkage factor:", round(shrinkage, 3), "\n")
Shrinkage factor: 0.3
Code 
cat("Bayes estimate of team strength:", round(theta_bayes, 3), "\n")
Bayes estimate of team strength: -2.764
Code 
cat("Current betting line: -3.5\n")
Current betting line: -3.5
Code 
theta_seq <- seq(-20, 10, length.out = 300)
prior_dens <- dnorm(theta_seq, 0, tau)
lik_dens   <- dnorm(theta_seq, ybar, sqrt(sig2n))
post_prec  <- 1/tau^2 + n_bears/s^2
post_mean  <- (ybar * n_bears / s^2) / post_prec
post_sd    <- 1 / sqrt(post_prec)
post_dens  <- dnorm(theta_seq, post_mean, post_sd)

plot(theta_seq, post_dens, type = "l", col = "firebrick", lwd = 2,
     ylim = c(0, max(post_dens, prior_dens, lik_dens) * 1.1),
     xlab = expression(theta), ylab = "Density",
     main = "Bears team strength: prior, likelihood, posterior")
lines(theta_seq, prior_dens, col = "gray50", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
lines(theta_seq, lik_dens / (sqrt(2 * pi * sig2n)), col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, lty = 3)
abline(v = -3.5, col = "darkgreen", lty = 4)
abline(v = theta_bayes, col = "firebrick", lty = 1)
legend("topright",
       legend = c("Posterior", "Prior N(0,16)", "Scaled likelihood", "Line = -3.5", "Bayes est"),
       col    = c("firebrick", "gray50", "steelblue", "darkgreen", "firebrick"),
       lty    = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 1), lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.75)

The Bayes shrinkage estimate is \(-2.76\), which is greater than the current line of \(-3.5\). This means the hierarchical model rates the Bears slightly better than the market. The shrinkage factor of 0.30 reflects the fact that nine games with a standard deviation of 18 points provides limited information relative to the pre-season prior. The two 50-point losses dominate the raw average, but the posterior appropriately discounts them.

The probability that the Bears cover the \(-3.5\) spread, under the posterior, is:

Code 
prob_cover <- pnorm(-3.5, mean = post_mean, sd = post_sd, lower.tail = FALSE)
cat("P(Bears cover -3.5 | data) =", round(prob_cover, 3), "\n")
P(Bears cover -3.5 | data) = 0.587

This is close to 50%, suggesting the line is roughly fair given the hierarchical analysis.
